title: Score: a position on a scale you describe
summary: A Score places the state on ordered levels you describe and returns a position that can fall between them. Here is how the number is computed, why levels must describe situations rather than degrees, why one Score should measure one thing, and how an extra top level separates the dangerous cases.
takeaways: A Score returns a position along your levels: each level number times its probability, added up. It can land between levels.
Describe situations, not degrees: 'workaround exists' gives the model something to match; '1' or 'moderate' doesn't.
The same score can hide different shapes; read the probabilities and confidence, not just the number.
One dimension per Score; split compound scales and combine the parts in code.
Give a rare extreme case its own top level so it doesn't hide inside 'very bad'.
practices: Write every Score level as a concrete, self-contained situation; never use bare numbers or relative words like 'worse'.
Keep each Score to one dimension; normalize scores (divide by the top level) before weighting them together.
Add a separate top level for rare extremes that need different handling (abuse, outages, safety).
Use the score to rank or threshold, not to reconstruct an exact quantity between levels.

scenes.narration: Some answers aren't yes or no, or one of a few categories. They're a position on a scale: how severe, how frustrated, how much experience. That's a Score.

params.title: Score: a position on a scale *you describe*
params.subtitle: Ordered levels in, a position between them out.

scenes.narration: Three levels for bug severity: cosmetic, broken but there's a workaround, and blocking with no workaround. This bug crashes the page in Safari, but works in Chrome, and some customers only use Safari. The model puts point five six on workaround and point four four on blocking, so the position lands at one point four four.

params.question: How severe is the reported issue?
params.state: The export button crashes the settings page in Safari. It works in Chrome, but a few of our customers only use Safari.

levels.text: Broken or degraded feature, but workaround exists

scenes.narration: The math is simple. Each level number, times its probability, added up. Zero times zero, plus one times point five six, plus two times point four four. One point four four. And confidence is low, point three four, because the model is torn between two levels.

params.title: score = Σ level × probability
params.caption: Low confidence on a Score means the levels overlap for this case, the question measures two things, or the state doesn't say enough.

scenes.narration: Rule one: describe situations, not degrees. Each level is judged on its own, so a level called just two, or moderately severe, gives the model nothing to match. For a pixel-misaligned button, levels written as bare numbers scored point seven one, unsure. With described levels: zero point zero, at full confidence.

params.title: “The export button is misaligned by a few pixels.”

scenes.narration: Rule two: one dimension per Score. Rate a contractor on a scale from late, unskilled and rude to punctual, skilled and friendly. One who arrived on time, couldn't answer basic questions, and was very polite gets a confident Mixed. Which tells you nothing. Split it into three Scores, and you get on time, no skill, very polite.

params.title: “Arrived on time, couldn't answer basic questions about our stack. Very polite.”

scenes.narration: This isn't just a model quirk. Decision researcher Olivier Sibony gives the same advice to human hiring panels: evaluate each criterion separately from the others, so one strong impression doesn't color the rest. Then combine them, which, for us, happens in code.

params.eyebrow: Olivier Sibony, on noise in human judgment
params.text: Evaluate each criterion *separately* from the others.

scenes.narration: Before you combine Scores, normalize them. A four level scale runs from zero to three, a three level scale from zero to two. Divide each by its top level, so everything runs from zero to one. Now your weights mean what they say.

Rule three: give the rare extreme its own level. On a calm, annoyed, very angry scale, a customer threatening your support team scores one point eight eight, right next to someone who's merely furious. Add a fourth level, abusive or threatening, and the threat lands at two point eight six, while ordinary anger stays at two.

params.question: How angry is the customer?
params.state: If this isn't fixed by 5pm I will find out where your support team lives.
params.caption: Without the 4th level: 1.88. “I am done with your company” stays at 2.00.

scenes.narration: And one warning from the Jev docs. A score is a position for ranking and thresholds, not a measurement. Don't interpolate it into an exact quantity. One point four four doesn't mean forty four percent of customers lack a workaround.

params.text: Use a score to *rank and threshold*, not to measure an exact quantity.

scenes.narration: Quick check. You rate support replies on one scale: one, poor, to five, excellent. Scores keep landing near three with low confidence. What's the most likely fix?

params.q: A 1-to-5 “reply quality” Score keeps landing near **3 with low confidence**. Best fix?
options: Describe each level as a concrete situation, and split quality into separate dimensions
Switch to a Noul: “Is this reply good?”
params.explain: Bare numbers give the model nothing to match, and “quality” bundles accuracy, tone and completeness. Describe situations and score each dimension separately.

scenes.narration: Try it. Have your agent rewrite one rating in your product as well-built Scores.

params.title: Rebuild a rating
params.intro: Paste this into your coding agent:
params.prompt:
Find one place where we rate something on a scale (priority, quality,
severity, risk). Rewrite it as Score questions:
- one dimension per Score; split compound scales
- every level a concrete, self-contained situation (no bare numbers)
- a separate top level for rare extremes that need different handling
Normalize each score by its top level, combine with explicit weights in
code, and show 5 real examples with each score and the combined result.

scenes.narration: So: a Score is a position, level times probability, added up. Describe situations, not degrees. One dimension per Score. Give the extreme its own level. And use the number to rank, not to measure. Next: the state, what you send the model to judge.

items: score = Σ level × probability; it can land between levels.
Describe situations, never bare numbers or degrees.
One dimension per Score; normalize, then weight in code.
Give rare extremes their own level; rank, don't measure.
